removed.text: The giant lies stretched out with his head in the corner (pokut) and his feet on the stove.
removed.reason: Misplaced, belongs in behavior_habitat: afanasyev1868:p.699 prints the giant lying with his head on the pokut and his feet on the stove; that is posture and setting, not a physical attribute.

downgraded.text: In the Voroneje tale the smith offers to forge her a new eye, ties her with a thick cord and puts out her sound eye with a red-hot awl.
downgraded.to_text: In the Voroneje tale the smith, asked by her to forge her an eye, ties her with a thick cord and puts out her sound eye with a red-hot awl.
downgraded.reason: On both pages she asks for the eye ("Make me an eye", ralston1873:p.179; "Скуй мнѣ глазъ", afanasyev1868:p.698); the smith does not offer it. afanasyev1868:p.698 has neither the thick cord nor the sound eye, so only Ralston supports the narrowed text.

retagged.text: In the Voroneje tale Likho is met in a dark, dense forest, reached along a small, narrow path.
retagged.reason: afanasyev1868:p.698 has the dense dark forest but not the small, narrow path; ralston1873:p.179 supports the whole clause.

flagged.reason: machal1918:p.252 prints "Licho" only as another name of the evil Dolya ("an evil Dolya (Nedolya, Licho)") in the Russian Dolya passage; the page does not tie it to the Likho of the tales, so whether it names this creature is a reading of the page.

The Russians row rests only on machal1918:pp.251-252, where Licho is a name of the evil Dolya in "Russian tradition"; the term maps to Russians under the table, but the page does not say the evil Dolya is the Likho of the tales.

grade_rationale.text: Ralston's Voroneje tale of One-eyed Likho is Afanasyev's tale III No. 14, and his Little-Russian variant is quoted by Afanasyev, so those passages count with Afanasyev, not as an independent source.
Afanasyev prints the Voroneje tale, the giant variants and the Little-Russian variant, and lists лихо among the words that stand for Недоля, with proverbs on it.

Ralston's account of Licho as an evil spirit among the Polish peasantry cites Wojcicki, not Afanasyev, and he records a proverb on Likho common to Poland and South Russia, giving Poles and Ukrainians.
Machal, citing no source on the page, records Licho as a name of the evil Dolya in Russian tradition, a third independent author (the identification with the tale figure is flagged).
The verified entry names three peoples (Russians, Poles, Ukrainians) across three independent authors, so the grade is widely-attested, though the tale itself rests on Afanasyev alone.
